notes:
Task and constraints: Find the cheapest flight from src to dst using at most K stops.
Idea: Search routes by accumulated price while tracking how many flights remain.
Technique and why it applies: A min-heap expands low-cost routes first; best stores a separate cost for each node and remaining-flight budget.
Invariant: Every heap entry represents a route candidate with its current price and remaining flight allowance.
Edge cases: K stops permits K+1 flights. The code checks negative allowance before accepting dst, so reaching the destination with no flights remaining is skipped.
Complexity: Up to O(nK) node-budget states and O(EK) transitions; heap work is roughly O(EK log(nK)), with O(nK+E) space.

Task and constraints: Count integers from 1 through n that rotate to a different valid number.
Idea: Rotate each decimal digit with a lookup table, reject invalid digits, then compare the result.
Technique and why it applies: Digits 0,1,8 stay unchanged; 2,5,6,9 change; 3,4,7 invalidate the number. The accumulated value reconstructs the rotated number.
Invariant: status remains true only when all processed digits have valid rotations, and temp accumulates their rotated place values.
Edge cases: Zero is excluded because it rotates to itself. Numbers containing any invalid digit stop processing immediately.
Complexity: For n candidates with at most D digits each, time is O(nD), with O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count positive integers at most N that rotate validly and change value.
Idea: Use digit dynamic programming to classify generated numbers as invalid, unchanged, or changed.
Technique and why it applies: Appending 0, 1, or 8 preserves a number's prior status; appending 2, 5, 6, or 9 marks it changed. Invalid digits are never generated.
Invariant: dp[x] records the rotation class of each generated number x.
Edge cases: dp[0] starts as SAME, and transitions are written only when the constructed value does not exceed N.
Complexity: The array has N+1 entries and each reachable prefix generates a constant number of transitions, giving O(N) time and O(N) space.

Task and constraints: Count numbers in the range whose digit rotation is valid and differs from the original.
Idea: Inspect each number's digit set and reject invalid digits while looking for a changing digit.
Technique and why it applies: Presence of 3, 4, or 7 invalidates rotation; presence of 2, 5, 6, or 9 guarantees change if no invalid digit occurs.
Invariant: result counts numbers with no invalid digit and at least one digit that changes.
Edge cases: Repeated digits do not matter because only set membership is needed. Numbers containing only 0, 1, and 8 are not counted.
Complexity: String conversion and set operations cost O(D) per candidate, giving O(ND) time and O(D) temporary space.

Task and constraints: Decide whether the player can reach a target before any ghost intercepts.
Idea: Compare the player's Manhattan distance to the target with every ghost's distance.
Technique and why it applies: Manhattan distance is the minimum number of four-directional grid moves. Escape is guaranteed only when every ghost is strictly farther from target.
Invariant: dist computes a shortest grid distance from a coordinate to the target.
Edge cases: A tie is unsafe because the comparison is strict. An empty ghosts list makes min() fail in this implementation, although the usual constraints provide ghosts.
Complexity: Each ghost is checked once, so time is O(g) and auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Check whether the player reaches target before every ghost.
Idea: Compute the player's Manhattan distance and require all ghosts to be strictly farther away.
Technique and why it applies: Four-directional movement makes Manhattan distance the shortest path length. A ghost no farther from target can intercept or arrive first.
Invariant: total is the player's minimum travel distance, and each generator term computes one ghost's distance.
Edge cases: A ghost at target makes the result false. Unlike a min-based approach, all() on an empty ghost list returns True.
Complexity: The method checks g ghosts once, taking O(g) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count tilings of a 2-by-n board using dominoes and trominoes modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Use the recurrence dp[i] = 2*dp[i-1] + dp[i-3] after seeded base cases.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence counts arrangements by how the right edge is covered, using symmetry and smaller-width subproblems.
Invariant: dp[i] stores the tiling count for the width represented by this code's zero-based indexing.
Edge cases: Values for the first three widths are prefilled, so small n returns directly without entering the loop.
Complexity: The recurrence loop performs O(n) constant-time updates and the array requires O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Reorder characters of s according to the priority order in order.
Idea: Assign each ordered character a priority and bubble-sort the characters using adjacent swaps.
Technique and why it applies: Earlier order characters receive larger priority values, so the comparison moves them ahead. Unlisted characters share priority zero and appear after listed characters.
Invariant: Each bubble-sort pass moves a high-priority character toward the front of the remaining unsorted portion.
Edge cases: The variable sorted shadows a built-in name but does not affect this code. Equal-priority characters are not swapped, preserving their relative order.
Complexity: Bubble sort takes O(|s|^2) time and O(|s|) space for the character list.

Task and constraints: Arrange s according to order while preserving every character occurrence.
Idea: Count characters, emit ordered characters with their multiplicities, then append unlisted characters.
Technique and why it applies: Counter records frequencies. Membership in set(S) separates characters governed by the custom order from those that should be appended afterward.
Invariant: result contains all copies of each processed ordered character, and the extension adds each remaining frequency once.
Edge cases: Ordered characters absent from s add empty strings. Correct ordering assumes order contains no repeated characters, as guaranteed by the task.
Complexity: Counting and output construction take O(|s|+|order|) expected time and O(|s|+alphabet) space.

Task and constraints: Count words in words that are subsequences of s.
Idea: Bucket each word by its next required character and advance matching words as s is scanned.
Technique and why it applies: Only words waiting for the current source character can advance. Completed one-character suffixes increase the count; other suffixes move to their next-character bucket.
Invariant: word_dict[c] stores suffixes whose next unmatched character is c.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used without an import in this snippet, so it must be supplied externally. Accessing w[0] also assumes words are nonempty.
Complexity: Suffix slicing may copy characters, so total work is proportional to total word length; bucket storage can also be linear in that total.

Task and constraints: Count words that appear as subsequences of S.
Idea: Store an iterator for each word in a bucket keyed by its next required character.
Technique and why it applies: For each source character, advance all waiting iterators once and place them in the bucket for their next character. Finished iterators use the None bucket.
Invariant: Each iterator points to the next unmatched character, and waiting[c] contains words awaiting c.
Edge cases: Empty words are immediately stored under None and counted. A source character advances only words that need that character.
Complexity: Each word character advances at most once, giving O(|S|+total word characters) time and O(total word characters) space.

Task and constraints: Determine the size of the preimage of the factorial trailing-zero function for k.
Idea: Count trailing zeros and binary-search for the largest n whose factorial has at most k zeros.
Technique and why it applies: Repeated division by five counts factors of five in n!. The difference between adjacent at-most boundaries gives the number of integers with exactly k zeros.
Invariant: Binary-search bounds narrow around the transition where the monotone zero count exceeds k.
Edge cases: The helper is also called with k-1, including -1 when k is zero; its boundary behavior must yield the expected difference.
Complexity: Each search uses O(log k) probes and each probe counts zeros in O(log n), for O(log k log n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Return five if some factorial has exactly K trailing zeros, otherwise return zero.
Idea: Binary-search for the first n whose factorial has at least K trailing zeros.
Technique and why it applies: Summing floor divisions by 5, 25, and higher powers counts trailing zeros. The preimage has size five when the lower-bound count equals K.
Invariant: left converges to the smallest integer whose factorial reaches at least K zeros.
Edge cases: K=0 returns five because 0! through 4! have no trailing zeros. The search upper bound is 5K.
Complexity: O(log K) binary-search steps each perform O(log K) divisions, giving O(log^2 K) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether a 3-by-3 tic-tac-toe board could arise during legal play.
Idea: Encode X as +1, O as -1, and blanks as zero; use the total to validate move parity.
Technique and why it applies: The signed sum distinguishes equal move counts from one extra X. The code then rejects a winning line for the player who could not have moved last.
Invariant: s is the flattened signed board and sm equals the number of X marks minus O marks.
Edge cases: The bit-shift test rejects impossible count differences among board totals. The board is assumed to contain only X, O, and spaces.
Complexity: A fixed nine-cell board and eight possible winning lines require O(1) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Decide whether a 3-by-3 tic-tac-toe board is reachable under alternating moves.
Idea: Count X and O marks and check their relationship to any winning line.
Technique and why it applies: X must have the same count as O or one additional mark. X wins only with one extra move; O wins only with equal counts.
Invariant: x_count and o_count describe the board, while win checks rows, columns, and diagonals.
Edge cases: The implementation does not explicitly reject simultaneous wins; some impossible boards may pass its separate count checks. Input is assumed to be a three-row board.
Complexity: The board is scanned a constant number of times, giving O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count subarrays whose maximum lies within inclusive bounds [left,right].
Idea: For each qualifying value, count subarrays where it is the maximum using nearest greater boundaries.
Technique and why it applies: A monotonic stack computes previous and next greater indices. The product of left choices and right choices counts subarrays with that index as a maximum.
Invariant: The boundary arrays delimit the region where nums[i] is maximal under the code's strict comparisons.
Edge cases: Equal maxima can be attributed to multiple indices because only strictly smaller stack values are popped, so duplicates may be double-counted. This approach is not generally correct for the bounded-maximum task.
Complexity: Stack construction and contribution summation take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Count subarrays whose maximum is between L and R inclusive.
Idea: Subtract subarrays with maximum at most L-1 from those with maximum at most R.
Technique and why it applies: count tracks the number of valid subarrays ending at each position. A value within the bound extends them; a value above the bound resets the running count.
Invariant: curr counts valid subarrays ending at the current position, and result accumulates these counts.
Edge cases: Values equal to either bound are handled correctly by the subtraction. The method assumes L is no greater than R.
Complexity: Two scans take O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether goal is a rightward cyclic rotation of s.
Idea: Rotate the string one position at a time and compare each result with goal.
Technique and why it applies: Every rotation appears within at most len(s) shifts. Each iteration constructs the next right rotation, then compares it with the target.
Invariant: s is the current right rotation generated from the original input.
Edge cases: Empty equal strings incorrectly return False because the loop executes zero times. Equal nonempty strings are found after a full rotation cycle.
Complexity: Each of n iterations constructs and compares O(n) characters, giving O(n^2) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether B is a rotation of A using a substring search.
Idea: Search for B in A+A using a custom Knuth-Morris-Pratt matcher.
Technique and why it applies: Every cyclic rotation appears as a length-|A| substring of the doubled string. KMP uses a prefix table to avoid rescanning matched text.
Invariant: j tracks the current matched pattern prefix, and prefix stores fallback positions for mismatches.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths return False immediately. Empty strings return True because strStr treats an empty needle as found and lengths match.
Complexity: KMP runs in O(|A|+|B|) time with O(|B|) prefix space, plus O(|A|) for A+A.

Task and constraints: Determine whether B is a cyclic rotation of A.
Idea: Require equal lengths and check whether B occurs in the doubled string A+A.
Technique and why it applies: All cyclic rotations of A appear as length-|A| substrings of A+A, so the membership test directly recognizes a rotation.
Invariant: The substring search succeeds exactly when B is present within the doubled sequence.
Edge cases: Equal empty strings return True under Python substring semantics. Unequal lengths are rejected before searching.
Complexity: Concatenation uses O(n) space, and substring search is typically linear, giving O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
